happened: On April 23, 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14281. It told federal agencies to stop enforcing disparate impact claims and to remove the idea from their regulations. The Justice Department removed disparate impact from its Title VI rules in December 2025, and Commerce, Interior, Transportation, Agriculture, FEMA, Education and GSA did the same in 2026.

key_dates.event: Executive Order 14281, "Restoring Equality of Opportunity and Meritocracy," signed.
Justice Department final rule removes disparate-impact liability from its Title VI regulations (90 FR 57141).
Office of Legal Counsel opinion finds EEOC disparate-impact guidelines unconstitutional.
GSA becomes the latest agency to remove disparate impact from its Title VI rules.

legal: No court ruling on the order or the agency rules was found. Laws and court decisions that recognize disparate impact (for example, under Title VII) were not changed by these actions.
closeness: Close to the regulatory path the chapter describes: an administration narrowing the doctrine through executive orders and regulations. Congress has not ended the doctrine by law, which the chapter named as the other option.
uncertain: HUD's proposals to remove disparate impact from its Fair Housing Act and Title VI rules were still pending as of August 2026. No lawsuit against the Justice Department rule was found; a May 2026 lawsuit over a separate CFPB lending rule was seen only in a secondary summary. Newest source is from August 2026.

happened: In 2025 the Luevano consent decree, which had limited written entrance tests for federal jobs since 1981, was ended: OPM asked the court to end it in March 2025, and the court dismissed the case on August 1, 2025. In September 2025, OPM finalized a 'Rule of Many' rule changing how job candidates are ranked. On July 31, 2026, OPM issued an interim final rule removing references to the Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures from federal hiring rules.

legal: The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (Judge Reggie B. Walton) dismissed Luevano v. Campbell on August 1, 2025, on a joint motion by the parties.

uncertain: Whether OPM has brought back governmentwide written entrance tests is not known. The July 2026 rule was open for comment until September 29, 2026. Newest source is from July 2026.

happened: OPM changed performance review rules twice. A rule effective October 15, 2025 lets OPM require a set spread of ratings for senior executives, citing a January 20, 2025 presidential memo. A rule effective August 6, 2026 does the same for General Schedule and blue-collar workers, ends grievances over ratings, and adds a required supervisory element for all supervisors.

key_dates.event: OPM final rule on Senior Executive Service performance ratings published (effective October 15, 2025).
OPM final rule on performance appraisal for GS and other employees published (effective August 6, 2026).

happened: OPM published a final rule on August 3, 2026, effective September 2, 2026, that ranks employees in a reduction in force mainly by performance ratings. Veterans' preference is added as extra points, and tenure and length of service are used only to break ties.

uncertain: No court ruling on the new rule was checked. Newest source is from September 2026.

happened: On January 20, 2025, Executive Order 14171 brought back the 2020 Schedule F order (EO 13957) under the new name "Schedule Policy/Career." OPM published the final rule on February 6, 2026. On June 3, 2026, an executive order moved about 8,000 employees, nearly all at GS-15 or above, into the category.

legal: NTEU v. Trump (U.S. District Court for D.C.) was paused while OPM wrote its rule; on March 17, 2026, the court let the union file an amended complaint once positions were moved. No injunction or merits ruling was found, per a March 2026 Congressional Research Service report.

uncertain: How many people are affected in practice, and whether any court has ruled since the June 2026 order, were not confirmed. Court status comes from the March 2026 CRS report. Newest source is from June 2026.

happened: On January 20, 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14171, which revoked President Biden's 2021 order and, according to OPM, restored the removal policies of the 2018 order (EO 13839); OPM proposed matching rules in July 2026. On March 27, 2025, Executive Order 14251 ended collective bargaining at many agencies. The Senate confirmed Charlton Allen as FLRA General Counsel in August 2026, and the Impasses Panel is fully staffed again.

legal: Unions sued over Executive Order 14251. The D.C. Circuit lifted an injunction in the NTEU case in 2025. On February 26, 2026, the Ninth Circuit vacated a nationwide preliminary injunction in AFGE v. Trump; other claims continue in district court. In May 2026, the First Circuit declined to pause a district court order requiring the VA to restore its AFGE contract. No final ruling on the merits was found.
closeness: The removal policies of EO 13839 were restored, the FLRA General Counsel was confirmed, and the Impasses Panel is staffed, as recommended. No order reissuing EOs 13836 (contracts) or 13837 (official time) was found; EO 14251 instead goes further by ending bargaining at many agencies.
uncertain: No order formally reissuing EOs 13836 and 13837 was found in the Federal Register. The July 2026 OPM rule is only proposed. Court cases over EO 14251 are still at the preliminary stage. Newest source is from August 2026.
